fuentes/periegesis-hecateo/resumen.texto: Description of the known world in two books, Europe and Asia, which according to tradition accompanied a map. It is lost, and some three hundred fragments survive, almost all of them short entries from the dictionary of Stephanus of Byzantium (collected by Jacoby as FGrHist 1). Three of them are the oldest surviving mention of the Celts: Massalia is “a city of Liguria, next to Celtica, a colony of the Phocaeans”, Narbo is “a Celtic market and city”, and Nyrax is “a Celtic city”.

fuentes/periegesis-hecateo/por_que_impor.texto: It shows that around 500 BC the Greeks already called the peoples of the interior of Massalia Celts (Keltoi), a name that, according to Caesar (BG I.1) and Pausanias (I.4.1), they used for themselves. These are quotations of quotations, abbreviated by a grammarian a thousand years later: it is not certain that the adjective “Celtic” comes from Hecataeus rather than from whoever summarized him, and they say nothing about what those peoples were like.

fuentes/sobre-el-oceano-piteas/resumen.texto: Account of Pytheas's voyage through the Atlantic: the coasts of Iberia and Gaul, the cape of the Ostimii (Brittany), the island of Britain, which he traveled around and measured, the tin mines of Belerion, the island of Thule six days' sail to the north, and a sea “curdled” where one could not sail. He measured the latitude of Massalia with the gnomon and the length of the days in the north. It is lost: we know it through fragments in Strabo (books I to IV), Pliny (II, IV and XXXVII), Geminus and, without being named, Diodorus (V.21-22).

fuentes/sobre-el-oceano-piteas/por_que_i.texto: It is the first description of Britain and of its inhabitants, and the origin of the name of the “Pretannic” islands. Polybius and Strabo called him a liar; modern criticism (Roseman 1994, Cunliffe 2001) shows that his latitude of Massalia is almost exact and that his reports on the tides and on the long days of the north are essentially correct, although Thule is still unidentified (Iceland, Norway or the Shetlands).

fuentes/etica-nicomaquea/resumen.texto: Aristotle's treatise on happiness and the virtues, compiled from his lectures at the Lyceum. Speaking of courage (III.7, 1115b), he says that whoever fears nothing, “neither earthquakes nor waves, as they say of the Celts”, is not brave but mad or insensible. In the Eudemian Ethics (III.1) he repeats the image of the Celts who take up arms against the waves, and in the Politics he counts them among the warlike peoples (VII.2) and says that they openly honor love between men (II.9).

fuentes/etica-nicomaquea/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the first Greek characterizations of the Celts, secondhand (“as they say”), and it fixes the commonplace of a courage without measure that borders on madness, which Ephorus, Nicolaus of Damascus and Aelian repeat and which Strabo (VII.2.1) already rejected. Plutarch (Camillus 22) tells that Aristotle also heard of the Celtic capture of Rome.

fuentes/etica-nicomaquea/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by D. P. Chase on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/leyes-platon/resumen.texto: Plato's last and longest dialogue, on the city and its laws, held between an Athenian, a Cretan and a Spartan. In book I (637d-e), discussing whether one should drink at banquets, the Athenian lists the warlike peoples who drink heavily: Scythians, Persians, Carthaginians, Celts, Iberians and Thracians.

fuentes/leyes-platon/por_que_importa.texto: It is the earliest mention of the Celts in a philosopher, and it shows that around 350 BC they already appeared in Athens on the list of warlike, heavy-drinking barbarians. There is no observation of his own: it is a commonplace that later authors will repeat about wine and the Gauls.

fuentes/leyes-platon/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Benjamin Jowett on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/historias-eforo/resumen.texto: The first universal Greek history, in thirty books, from the return of the Heraclidae to the siege of Perinthus (340 BC); it is lost. Strabo preserves what it said about the Celts: that together with the Scythians, the Indians and the Ethiopians they were one of the four great peoples at the ends of the world (I.2.28); that Celtica reached as far as Gades; that they were friends of the Greeks and punished a young man who grew fatter than the measure of a belt (IV.4.6); and that, to exercise courage, they let the sea destroy their houses (VII.2.1). The Periplus of Pseudo-Scymnus also summarizes it.

fuentes/historias-eforo/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the Greek image of the 4th century BC: the Celts as an enormous and distant people of the west, placed in a geographical scheme rather than known from direct knowledge. Strabo warns that much of what Ephorus said “does not hold for the people of today” (IV.4.6) and, following Posidonius, rejects the story about the waves.

fuentes/helenicas-jenofonte/resumen.texto: History of Greece in seven books that continues Thucydides from 411 BC to the battle of Mantinea (362 BC). In book VII (1.20-22 and 1.28) he tells that Dionysius I of Syracuse sent ships to Sparta in 369 and 368 BC carrying Celts, Iberians and horsemen, who harassed the Thebans and their allies with cavalry charges and quick retreats near Corinth and Sicyon.

fuentes/helenicas-jenofonte/por_que_impo.texto: It is the earliest mention of Celts in a Greek historian who writes about his own time, and it shows that at the start of the 4th century BC they already served as mercenaries in the Mediterranean, recruited by Syracuse. Xenophon, a sympathizer of Sparta, describes them only as effective auxiliary troops.

fuentes/helenicas-jenofonte/leer.0.titul.texto: English translation by H. G. Dakyns on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/historias-timeo/resumen.texto: History of Sicily and the Greek West in thirty-eight books, from mythical times to the death of Agathocles (289 BC), with a separate work on Pyrrhus that reached 264 BC; both are lost. From quotations we know that he said the Celts of the Atlantic coast worshipped the Dioscuri (Diodorus IV.56) and that tin was brought from an island, Mictis, six days' sail from Britain (Pliny IV.104). Probably the myth of Galates, son of Heracles and a Celtic princess, as ancestor of the Galatians, is also his (Diodorus V.24).

fuentes/historias-timeo/por_que_importa.texto: He was the main Greek source on the West before Polybius, and many reports on the Celts and on Britain reached Diodorus through him, possibly taken from Pytheas. Polybius (book XII) attacked him for writing from libraries, without seeing the places or speaking with witnesses.

fuentes/himno-a-delos/resumen.texto: Hymn in hexameters, the fourth of Callimachus's hymns, on the birth of Apollo on the island of Delos. Apollo, still in his mother's womb, prophesies that one day the “late titans” of the far west, the Celts, will fall upon Greece and threaten his temple at Delphi, and that their shields will be the prize of Ptolemy, who will defeat them by the Nile (vv. 171-190). It alludes to the attack on Delphi of 279 BC and to Ptolemy II's repression of his rebellious Galatian mercenaries, who, according to Pausanias (I.7.2), were abandoned on an island of the Nile until they died.

fuentes/himno-a-delos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the literary testimony closest to the invasion of 279 BC, and it shows how the Ptolemaic court turned the Galatians into giant enemies of the gods, a model that Pergamon later used in its monuments. It is poetic propaganda, not narrative.

fuentes/himno-a-delos/leer.0.titulo.texto: Hymns 4 to 6 in the English translation by A. W. Mair (1921), on Theoi

fuentes/argonauticas/resumen.texto: Epic poem in four books on the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece. On the return (book IV) the heroes go up the Eridanus and the Rhone, near the lakes of the Celts, and Apollonius records what “the Celts tell”: that the amber carried by those rivers is the tears Apollo shed when he was banished from heaven.

fuentes/argonauticas/por_que_importa.texto: It shows Celtica as the mythical edge of the Greek world in the 3rd century BC, and it preserves what is presented as a Celtic tradition associated with Apollo, although it is not known where the poet took it from.

fuentes/argonauticas/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by R. C. Seaton on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/sobre-las-cosas-maravillosas/res.texto: Collection of 178 reports of marvels attributed to Aristotle but compiled by others, in layers, between the 3rd century BC and the 2nd century AD. It includes a “road of Heracles” that ran from Italy to the land of the Celts, the Celtoligurians and the Iberians, and that the peoples along it protected travelers (85); that the Celts hunted with a poison they called “toxic” (86); and that Celtic tin melts more easily than lead (50).

fuentes/sobre-las-cosas-maravillosas/por.texto: It preserves reports on roads and trade in the western Mediterranean in the Hellenistic period, mixed with fables, and it shows Celtica as a land of wonders. Its date and sources are uncertain; Timaeus is one of the most likely.

fuentes/historias-polibio/resumen.texto: History in forty books, of which the first five survive complete, of Rome's rise between 264 and 146 BC. Book II (14-35) is the oldest and most complete account of the Gauls of Italy: their settlement in the Po valley, their life in villages without walls, with wealth in cattle and gold and power measured by the number of companions (II.17), the sack of Rome, the wars of the 3rd century, the battle of Telamon with the Gaesatae who fought naked (II.28-31) and the swords that bent at the first blow (II.33). Book III follows the Gauls who joined Hannibal, and fragments of later books speak of the Galatians of Asia, of Chiomara (XXI.38) and of the “war of fire” against the Celtiberians (XXXV.1).

fuentes/historias-polibio/por_que_import.texto: It is the closest and best-informed source on the Celts of Italy, written by someone who traveled through the Alps and spoke with witnesses. But Polybius writes to explain Roman success, and he shares the judgment of the aristocracy that protected him: the Gauls fail because they are guided by impulse (thymos) and not by reason (II.35), a commonplace that must be separated from the data.

fuentes/historias-polibio/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book II (the Gauls of Italy), English translation by Shuckburgh (Perseus)

fuentes/historias-posidonio/resumen.texto: History in fifty-two books that continued Polybius's from 146 BC, now lost entirely. Literal quotations about the Celts survive in Athenaeus (IV.36-40, from book XXIII: the banquets seated on skins, the champion's portion and the duels at the table, the Arvernian king Luernius who scattered gold from his chariot, and the bards; and VI.246) and in Strabo (IV.4.5: the heads nailed to the doors, which he himself saw and to which he says he became accustomed). Many scholars believe that he is also, without naming him, the source of Diodorus V.25-32 and of Strabo IV.4.

fuentes/historias-posidonio/por_que_impo.texto: It is the closest thing to fieldwork that antiquity left on the Celts: a philosopher who traveled, observed and asked questions. But how much can be attributed to him is a debated hypothesis: Tierney (1960) assigned him almost all the ancient ethnography of the Gauls, including much of Caesar's; Nash (1976) argued that the coincidences do not prove a common source, that Caesar is independent, and that Posidonius described mainly southern Gaul around 100 BC. The edition by Edelstein and Kidd accepts as fragments only the passages that name him.

fuentes/biblioteca-historica-diodoro-lib.texto: Book V, devoted to the islands and the peoples of the west and north, describes Britain and the tin trade (21-22), the Celtiberians and Lusitanians (33-34) and, in chapters 25 to 32, the Gauls: their cold land, their fondness for wine, which Italian merchants exchange at the rate of one amphora per slave (26), the gold dedicated in sanctuaries that no one touches (27), their appearance, their banquets and their Pythagorean belief in immortality, for which they throw letters to the dead onto the pyres (28), the chariots and the embalmed heads of enemies (29), the weapons (30), and the bards, the diviners and the druids, “philosophers and theologians” without whom no sacrifice is made (31). He adds that the inland peoples are properly Celts and those farther north are Galatians, and that some Britons of Iris (Ireland) eat human flesh (32).

It is the most complete ancient description of the Gauls, but Diodorus never set foot in Gaul: he compiles, according to the most widespread view although without naming him, above all Posidonius (Tierney 1960; Nash 1976 disputes this), and for Britain probably Timaeus and Pytheas, with the anachronisms that brings. It shows the Greek portrait of the Gaul around 100 BC, which can be contrasted with archaeology: the trade in Italian wine, for example, is confirmed by the thousands of amphorae found in Gaul.
Book V in the English translation by George Booth (1814 edition), on Wikisource

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-iii/.texto: Description of Iberia. It presents the Turdetani of the south as the most civilized (III.2) and the peoples of the north and interior (Gallaecians, Astures, Cantabrians and Lusitanians) as mountain people who drink water, sleep on the ground, eat acorn bread, wash with urine, and sacrifice goats, horses and prisoners to a god of war (III.3.7, III.4.16). It says that the Celtiberians and their northern neighbors worship a nameless god on nights of full moon, that some call the Gallaecians “godless” (III.4.16), and that among the Cantabrians the daughters inherit and give wives to their brothers (III.4.18).

It is the basis of almost everything said about Celtic Hispania, but Strabo did not visit the peninsula: he follows Polybius, Posidonius and Artemidorus, and arranges the peoples on a scale that runs from urban life, which is good, to the mountains, which are wild, to show that Rome civilizes them. What he calls Cantabrian “gynecocracy” is his reading of inheritance and dowry customs, and it does not prove a matriarchy.
English translation by Hamilton and Falconer on Wikisource
Book III, English translation by Hamilton and Falconer (Perseus)

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-iv/r.texto: Description of Gaul, Britain, Ireland and the Alps. He tells how the Gauls learned from Massalia to write their contracts in Greek (IV.1.5) and discusses the origin of the gold of Tolosa (IV.1.13, according to Timagenes and Posidonius). In a passage that in part quotes and in part seems to follow Posidonius (IV.4.2-6), he describes the Gauls as “mad for war”, impetuous but simple and without malice; he distinguishes three honored classes, bards, vates and druids; and he speaks of severed heads, of the colossus of straw and wood in which victims were burned (sacrifices that, he says, the Romans put an end to, IV.4.5), and of the women of the Namnetes who lived on an island. Of the inhabitants of Ireland he says that they eat human flesh and have intercourse with their mothers and sisters, but he notes that he has no trustworthy witnesses (IV.5.4).

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-iv/p.texto: Strabo writes in the time of Augustus and Tiberius, with Gaul already pacified: he puts in the past what he tells about the Gauls and presents it as barbarism that Rome corrected. It is the best example of how an observation by Posidonius becomes a commonplace, although Strabo himself marks his doubts.

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-iv/l.texto: English translation by Hamilton and Falconer on Wikisource
Book IV, chapter 4 (the Gauls), English translation by Hamilton and Falconer (Perseus)

fuentes/geografia-de-estrabon-libro-vii/.texto: Describes Germany, the Danube and the Balkans. He criticizes those who said that the Cimbri took up arms against the tide, or that the Celts let the sea destroy their houses to exercise courage, as Ephorus did, and sides with Posidonius, who rejected those tales (VII.2.1). He speaks of the Boii, Scordisci and Taurisci of the Danube, of the defeat of the Boii by Burebista's Dacians and of the “desert of the Boii” (VII.3.11, VII.5.2), and he preserves, according to Ptolemy I, the reply of the Celts to Alexander: that they feared only that the sky might fall on them (VII.3.8).

It is one of the main sources on the Celts of central Europe and the Danube, which few authors describe. For the episode of Alexander it cites a direct witness, which makes it more reliable than most anecdotes about the Celts.
English translation by Hamilton and Falconer on Wikisource
Book VII, 3.8 (the Celts and Alexander), English translation by H. L. Jones (Perseus)

fuentes/anabasis-de-alejandro-arriano/re.texto: History of the campaigns of Alexander the Great in seven books, based above all on the memoirs of Ptolemy I and Aristobulus, who took part in them. In the Danube campaign of 335 BC (I.4.6-8) he tells that envoys came from the Celts of the Ionian Gulf, very tall and with a high opinion of themselves; Alexander asked them what they feared most, expecting them to say him, and they replied that they feared the sky might fall on them, but that they valued his friendship above all. Alexander declared them friends and remarked that the Celts were braggarts. In VII.15.4 he mentions another Celtic embassy, in Babylon, in 323 BC.

fuentes/anabasis-de-alejandro-arriano/po.texto: It is the account of the first documented diplomatic contact between Celts and Greeks. It comes from a witness (Ptolemy, cited by name by Strabo VII.3.8) through Arrian, who follows him in general. The phrase about the sky became an emblem of Celtic pride; its original sense is debated.

fuentes/anabasis-de-alejandro-arriano/le.texto: English translation by E. J. Chinnock on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/periplo-pseudo-escimno/resumen.texto: Description of the coasts of the world in iambic verse, dedicated to a King Nicomedes of Bithynia at the end of the 2nd century BC and attributed for centuries, without foundation, to Scymnus of Chios. It follows Ephorus, Timaeus and Eratosthenes, and preserves Ephorus's image of the Celts as the greatest people of the west, reaching to the ocean, with customs similar to the Greeks' and friendly to them.

fuentes/periplo-pseudo-escimno/por_que_i.texto: It is an indirect witness to what Ephorus said about the Celts in the 4th century BC. It adds no information of its own.

fuentes/decreto-de-cos-sobre-delfos/titu.texto: Decree of Cos on the salvation of Delphi

fuentes/decreto-de-cos-sobre-delfos/resu.texto: Decree of the city of Cos, in the Dodecanese, approved in 278 BC, which orders a delegation to be sent to Delphi and sacrifices to be held, because the barbarians who had marched against the Greeks and against the sanctuary were punished by the god and by the men who came to defend it, and the temple was saved and adorned with the arms of the attackers.

fuentes/decreto-de-cos-sobre-delfos/por_.texto: It is the document closest to the Gaulish attack on Delphi, written months later, and it shows that the version of divine punishment spread at once. It describes the attackers only as “barbarians”.

fuentes/virtudes-de-mujeres-plutarco/res.texto: Treatise from the Moralia, dedicated to Cleo, which gathers stories of brave women to show that women's virtue is the same as men's. It includes the Celtic women who mediated between their peoples at war, which is why the treaty with Hannibal provided that complaints against the Celts would be judged by them (6); the Galatian Camma, priestess of Artemis, who poisoned at her wedding the murderer of her husband and died with him (20); and Chiomara, wife of the tetrarch Ortiagon, who had the Roman centurion who had raped her killed and brought his head to her husband, a story that Polybius heard her tell herself at Sardis (22).

fuentes/virtudes-de-mujeres-plutarco/por.texto: It is the main source for two of the few Celtic women with a name and a story of their own, and for a much-cited fact about the public role of Celtic women. These are moralizing tales chosen to support an argument, and the mediation by Celtic women is recounted by Plutarch alone.

fuentes/descripcion-de-grecia-pausanias/.texto: Guide in ten books to the sanctuaries, cities and monuments of Greece. It recounts twice the Galatian invasion of 279 BC: in book I (3-4), in connection with a painting of the battle in Athens, and in book X (19-23), in detail: the passage of Thermopylae, the atrocities at Callium, the attack on Delphi repelled with earthquakes, lightning, snow and the apparitions of heroes, and the death of Brennus. He explains the tactic of the trimarkisia, groups of three horsemen, “because the Celts call a horse a marka” (X.19.11), and speaks of the Galatians of Asia, whom the people of Pergamon kept away from the coast (I.4.5-6), of the figures Attalus dedicated on the Acropolis of Athens with the defeat of the Galatians in Mysia alongside those of giants, Amazons and Persians (I.25.2), and of the Galatian mercenaries of Ptolemy II (I.7.2).

Pausanias saw the votive offerings of the victory at Delphi and Athens, and he preserves a genuine Gaulish word. But he writes four centuries later and presents the invasion as a new war against the Persians, miracles included: it is the Greek memory of the event, not a chronicle.
Book X, 19 (the Galatians at Delphi), translation by Jones and Ormerod (Perseus)
Book I, 4 (the invasion and the Galatians of Asia), translation by Jones and Ormerod (Perseus)

fuentes/historia-romana-apiano/resumen.texto: History of Rome arranged by peoples and regions, in twenty-four books, of which the book on Spain, the book on Hannibal and the books on the civil wars survive, among others. The book on Spain is the main source for the Celtiberian and Lusitanian wars: Segeda, the massacres of Lucullus at Cauca and of Galba against the Lusitanians, Viriathus and the siege of Numantia (Iberia 44-98). Of the book on the Gauls (Celtica) there survive fragments on the sack of Rome, the Cimbri and Caesar's war.

fuentes/historia-romana-apiano/por_que_i.texto: Without Appian we would know almost nothing about Viriathus and Numantia, but he writes three centuries later and summarizes earlier sources, above all Polybius, without always saying which; his figures and chronology need checking. It is the version of the victors, although he criticizes the abuses of some Roman generals.

fuentes/historia-romana-apiano/leer.0.ti.texto: The Spanish Wars, English translation by Horace White (Perseus)

fuentes/historia-romana-apiano/leer.1.ti.texto: Fragments of the Gallic history, translation by White (Perseus)

fuentes/deipnosofistas/resumen.texto: Fictional conversation among scholars at a dinner in Rome, in fifteen books, on food, wine, luxury and customs, stocked with more than a thousand quotations from authors, most of them lost. In book IV (36-40; 151e-154c) he copies Posidonius: the Celts eat sitting on skins around low tables, take the meat with their hands, the rich drink pure wine and the poor drink wheat beer with honey; Luernius, king of the Arverni, scattered gold from his chariot and gave feasts in an enormous enclosure; in the past the bravest man kept the thigh, and whoever disputed it fought to the death. He also cites Phylarchus on the year-long banquet of the Galatian Ariamnes (IV.150d-f) and Posidonius on the parasites and bards of the Celts (VI.246c-d).

fuentes/deipnosofistas/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source that quotes Posidonius most literally on the Celts (Strabo summarizes and comments on him), and therefore the basis for measuring how much of Diodorus and Strabo comes from him. Athenaeus chooses what serves his theme, food and excess, so the portrait he leaves is partial by construction.

fuentes/deipnosofistas/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by C. D. Yonge (Perseus)

fuentes/historia-romana-dion-casio/resum.texto: History of Rome in eighty books, preserved in part and the rest in Byzantine summaries. It recounts Caesar's campaigns in Gaul (XXXVIII-XL), the conquest of Britain by Claudius (LX.19-22), the revolt of Boudica, whom he describes as tall, with a harsh voice and reddish hair, with an invented speech, a hare released to foretell the outcome, and atrocities against Roman women in the grove of the goddess Andraste (LXII.1-12), and the campaigns of Septimius Severus against the Caledonians and Maeatae, with the reply of Argentocoxos's wife to the empress Julia Domna on the sexual freedom of British women (LXXVI.12-16; LXXVII in the numbering of the Loeb edition).

fuentes/historia-romana-dion-casio/por_q.texto: It is the most detailed source on Boudica and northern Britain in the early third century. But he writes a century and a half after Boudica, follows the rhetorical model of Thucydides and makes barbarians speak in order to criticize Rome; he also calls the Germans “Celts” and the Gauls “Galatians.”

fuentes/historia-romana-dion-casio/leer..texto: Volume 5 of the English translation by H. B. Foster (years 54 to 211, with Boudica and Severus in Britain)

fuentes/geografia-de-ptolomeo/resumen.texto: Handbook in eight books for drawing the map of the world, with the coordinates of some eight thousand places. Book II gives the cities, rivers, capes and peoples of Ireland (II.2), Britain (II.3), Hispania (II.4-6), Gaul (II.7-10) and Germany (II.11), and book V those of Galatia (V.4). His Ireland, with some sixteen peoples, among them the Brigantes and the Menapii, and rivers such as the Senus (Shannon), is the oldest description of the island's interior.

fuentes/geografia-de-ptolomeo/por_que_im.texto: It preserves hundreds of place names and Celtic tribal names that are found nowhere else, and it is the basis for maps of pre-Roman peoples. Ptolemy compiled itineraries and the work of Marinus of Tyre, with large errors of position (Scotland bent eastward) and data from different dates that cannot be separated.

fuentes/vidas-de-los-filosofos-ilustres/.texto: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers

History of Greek philosophy in ten books, arranged by biographies and schools. In the prologue (I.1 and I.6) he records the view that philosophy began among the barbarians (the Persian magi, the Chaldeans, the gymnosophists of India and, among the Celts and Galatians, the so-called druids and semnotheoi), according to the Magicus attributed to Aristotle and book XXIII of Sotion, and he says that the druids taught in riddles: to honor the gods, not to do evil, and to practice courage.

It preserves the idea, circulating since the third century BC, of the druid as philosopher, and the threefold maxim that recurs in reconstructions of their doctrine. Diogenes himself rejects that thesis and holds that philosophy was born among the Greeks.
Prologue, English translation by R. D. Hicks (Perseus)
Book I (with the prologue), English translation by Hicks on Wikisource

fuentes/refutacion-de-todas-las-herejias.texto: Work in ten books that seeks to show that every Christian heresy derives from a pagan philosophy or cult. Book I summarizes the Greek philosophers and the barbarians: the Brahmins and the druids of the Celts, who according to the author studied Pythagorean philosophy thoroughly, which was taught to them by Zalmoxis, a Thracian slave of Pythagoras, who foretell the future by calculations and numbers and who practice magic (I.25; I.22 in the nineteenth-century English translation).
It shows how Christian authors inherited the Hellenistic image of the Pythagorean druid, without any new information. The attribution to Hippolytus is disputed.
Volume I of the English translation by F. Legge (Philosophumena)
Book I, English translation of the Ante-Nicene Fathers (New Advent)

fuentes/stromata/resumen.texto: Work in eight books on the relation between the Christian faith and Greek philosophy. In book I (15.71) Clement holds that philosophy first flourished among the barbarians and lists the prophets of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans of Assyria, the druids of the Gauls, the Samanaeans of Bactria, the philosophers of the Celts, the magi of Persia and the gymnosophists of India.

fuentes/stromata/por_que_importa.texto: It is another link in the tradition of the druid as philosopher, used here to diminish the originality of the Greeks. It adds no data about real druids.

fuentes/stromata/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book I, English translation of the Ante-Nicene Fathers (New Advent)

fuentes/discursos-dion-crisostomo/resume.texto: Speech delivered at Prusa when declining an office, in which Dio holds that wise peoples place philosophers beside kings: the Persians place the magi, the Egyptians the priests, the Indians the Brahmins, and the Celts the druids, who deal with divination and all wisdom, without whom kings cannot do or decide anything, to the point that the druids are the ones who rule and the kings, seated on golden thrones, are their servants (49.7-8).

fuentes/discursos-dion-crisostomo/por_qu.texto: It is the most exaggerated version of the political power of the druids, which some read as confirmation of Caesar (VI.13). Dio did not know druids: he uses them as an example in an argument for the philosopher as counselor, and that rhetorical use invites caution in taking it as data.

fuentes/heracles-luciano/resumen.texto: Brief introductory speech in which Lucian says he saw in Gaul a painting of Heracles, whom the Celts called Ogmios: an old, bald and wrinkled man, with a lion skin and a club, who drags along a happy crowd with thin chains of gold and amber that come out of his tongue and hook onto their ears. A Celt who spoke Greek explained to him that for them eloquence is not Hermes but Heracles, because he is stronger, and that it ripens in old age.

fuentes/heracles-luciano/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only description of an image of Ogmios, a Gaulish god also named on two curse tablets from Bregenz, who is linked to the Irish Ogma. But it is a rhetorical prologue in which Lucian, already old, justifies his continuing to give lectures: the painting and the interpreter may be literary invention.

fuentes/heracles-luciano/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume III of the English translation by H. W. and F. G. Fowler, with “Heracles”

fuentes/zeuxis-luciano/resumen.texto: Speech in which Lucian, to explain that the public applauds novelty more than art, tells the story of the painter Zeuxis and that of Antiochus I, who defeated the Galatians because his sixteen elephants frightened the horses and the Gallic chariots, which had never seen such animals (8-11). Antiochus, he says, wept after the victory because he owed it to sixteen beasts.

fuentes/zeuxis-luciano/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source for the “battle of the elephants” (around 275-270 BC), written four centuries later as an illustrative anecdote, without a precise place or date.

fuentes/historias-varias-eliano/resumen.texto: Collection in fourteen books of anecdotes, curiosities and sayings of persons and peoples, taken from earlier authors. In book XII (22-23) he says that the Celts are the boldest of men, that they consider it shameful to flee a house that collapses or catches fire, and that some take up arms against the waves of the sea that carry them away.

fuentes/historias-varias-eliano/por_que_.texto: It is the last link in the topos of the Celts who fight against the sea, which runs from Aristotle and Ephorus to Nicolaus of Damascus and Aelian, and which Posidonius and Strabo (VII.2.1) had already rejected. It shows how a secondhand report was copied for five centuries.

fuentes/contra-celso/resumen.texto: Reply in eight books to “The True Word,” an attack on the Christians written by the philosopher Celsus around 175-180 and known only through Origen's quotations. In book I (16) he reproduces Celsus's list of ancient and wise peoples whose doctrines were akin to his own (the Galactophagi of Homer, the druids of the Gauls, the Getae), and he reproaches him for leaving out the Jews.

fuentes/contra-celso/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that in the second century the druids figured in the learned list of wise barbarians that pagan philosophers set against Christianity. It provides no information about their doctrine.

fuentes/contra-celso/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book I, English translation of the Ante-Nicene Fathers (New Advent)

fuentes/etnica-esteban-de-bizancio/resum.texto: Geographical dictionary of cities, peoples and regions, in some fifty books, which survives only in a later summary and in some fragments. Each entry gives the name, the ethnic adjective and a quotation from an author who used it, often a lost one: this is how the fragments of Hecataeus of Miletus on Massalia and Nyrax in Celtica survive, along with many names of Gallic, Iberian and Galatian peoples and cities.

fuentes/etnica-esteban-de-bizancio/por_q.texto: Without this dictionary we would not have the first mention of the Celts. The quotations are abbreviated and sometimes distorted by transmission, which requires reading them with caution.

fuentes/segundo-libro-de-los-macabeos/au.texto: Anonymous Jewish author (abridgement of Jason of Cyrene)

fuentes/segundo-libro-de-los-macabeos/re.texto: Jewish book in Greek that abridges the history of the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, which Jason of Cyrene wrote in five books now lost. Before a battle, Judas Maccabeus reminds his men of God's help in the past, among other things “the battle fought in Babylonia against the Galatians,” when eight thousand Jews with four thousand Macedonians defeated one hundred and twenty thousand (8:20).

fuentes/segundo-libro-de-los-macabeos/po.texto: It is one of the few reports of Jewish soldiers fighting Galatians in the service of the Seleucids, in the third century BC; no other source confirms it, and the figures are symbolic. It is canonical for Catholics and Orthodox, not for Jews or Protestants.

fuentes/segundo-libro-de-los-macabeos/le.texto: Chapter 8, Greek, Latin and English text (New Advent)

fuentes/pro-fonteio/resumen.texto: Speech by Cicero in defense of Marcus Fonteius, governor of Transalpine Gaul, accused of extortion by the Allobroges and the Volcae; it survives incomplete. Since he cannot deny all the charges, Cicero attacks the witnesses: the Gauls fear no gods and respect no oaths, they still make human sacrifices, they are the same people who besieged the Capitol and plundered Delphi, and they walk through the forum in their sagi and trousers, full of arrogance (especially 27-33).

fuentes/pro-fonteio/por_que_importa.texto: It is the clearest example of how the stereotype of the barbarian Gaul was used as a weapon in a courtroom: one of the first Latin mentions of Gallic human sacrifice comes from the mouth of an interested advocate. It also serves as a document, told by the defense, of a governor's abuses in the province.

fuentes/de-divinatione/resumen.texto: Dialogue in two books between Cicero and his brother Quintus on whether divination is real: Quintus defends it in book I and Marcus refutes it in book II. Among Quintus's examples are the druids (I.90): “there are some in Gaul, and I myself knew one, the Aeduan Diviciacus, your guest and admirer, who claimed to know nature, what the Greeks call physics, and foretold the future by omens and by conjecture.”

fuentes/de-divinatione/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only testimony from someone who dealt with a named druid, and it presents him as a sage comparable to Greek diviners, not as a bloodthirsty priest. But the sentence belongs to the character who defends divination, and Caesar, who knew Diviciacus much better, never calls him a druid.

fuentes/de-divinatione/leer.1.titulo.texto: Book I in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/cartas-a-atico/resumen.texto: More than four hundred letters from Cicero to his friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, published after Cicero's death. In 54 BC, while his brother Quintus accompanied Caesar on the second expedition to Britain, Cicero writes that it was already known that the island had not a single gram of silver and no booty but slaves, “among whom I do not expect you to find any who are educated in letters or music” (IV.16.7); in other letters he comments on the news of the Gallic war.

fuentes/cartas-a-atico/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how Britain looked from Rome: a poor land, of interest only for military and propaganda purposes, whose inhabitants were assumed to be without culture. It is a secondhand opinion, based on letters from the front.

fuentes/cartas-a-atico/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book IV in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/libro-viii-de-hircio/titulo.texto: Commentaries on the Gallic War, Book VIII

fuentes/libro-viii-de-hircio/resumen.texto: Continuation of Caesar's commentaries, written by his officer Aulus Hirtius, covering the years 51 and 50 BC: the last resistance of the Bituriges, the Carnutes, the Bellovaci under Correus, and the Cadurci under Lucterius and Drappes at Uxellodunum, whose defenders Caesar ordered to have their hands cut off (VIII.44), and the final pacification. In the preface, addressed to Balbus, Hirtius explains that he wrote it to complete Caesar's work.

fuentes/libro-viii-de-hircio/por_que_imp.texto: It closes the account of the conquest in the same tone of defense of Caesar: Hirtius justifies the punishment at Uxellodunum as a necessary deterrent, compatible with the well-known “clemency” of his commander. It is the only source for the last phase of the war.

fuentes/libro-viii-de-hircio/leer.0.titu.texto: English translation by McDevitte and Bohn (Perseus)

fuentes/epitome-de-justino/titulo.texto: Epitome of the Philippic Histories of Pompeius Trogus

fuentes/epitome-de-justino/resumen.texto: Summary in forty-four books of the lost universal history of Pompeius Trogus. It recounts the migration of the Gauls because of overpopulation and their arrival in Italy and Pannonia (XX.5, XXIV.4), the invasion of Macedonia and Greece and Brennus's attack on Delphi, repelled by an earthquake and a storm (XXIV.4-8), the crossing of the Galatians into Asia (XXV.2), the gold of Delphi at Toulouse (XXXII.3), and the founding of Massalia by the Phocaeans, with the marriage of Protis and Gyptis, daughter of the king of the Segobriges, and the Gauls learning from the Greeks to live in cities, cultivate the vine and be governed by laws (XLIII.3-5). At the end, Trogus recounts his own Vocontian lineage (XLIII.5.11-12).

fuentes/epitome-de-justino/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most complete version of the Celtic invasion of the Balkans and of the founding of Massalia according to the Greek tradition. That the author was a Gaul does not change the perspective: Gaul became so civilized that “it did not seem that Greece had migrated to Gaul, but Gaul to Greece” (XLIII.4.2). What we read has passed through two filters, Trogus and Justin's epitome, of uncertain date.

fuentes/epitome-de-justino/leer.0.titulo.texto: Books XXI to XXX (the invasion of Greece), English translation by J. S. Watson (1853)

fuentes/epitome-de-justino/leer.1.titulo.texto: Books XLI to XLIV (Massalia and the lineage of Trogus), translation by Watson

fuentes/hechos-y-dichos-memorables/resum.texto: Collection in nine books of exemplary anecdotes about Romans and foreigners, arranged by virtues and vices and dedicated to Tiberius. In the chapter on ancient customs (II.6.10-11) he says that the Gauls lent money to be repaid in the next world, because they believed in the immortality of the soul (“I would call them fools if these trouser-wearing barbarians did not think as Pythagoras did in his cloak”), and that the Cimbri and Celtiberians rejoiced in battle, because they died with glory, and lamented in sickness.

fuentes/hechos-y-dichos-memorables/por_q.texto: It shows the topos of the Gallic belief in immortality, already present in Caesar and Diodorus, turned into a moral anecdote. It has no source of its own.

fuentes/corografia-mela/resumen.texto: Description of the world in three books, written around 43-44, when Claudius was undertaking the conquest of Britain, which Mela mentions as imminent. On the Gauls (III.18-19) he says that they are proud and superstitious, that human sacrifices have been abolished but they still wound the consecrated at the altar, that the druids teach in secret for twenty years, in caves or remote groves, and that only one of their teachings was made public, so that they would be braver in war: that the soul is eternal; therefore they burn with the dead the things they used in life and send them accounts and debts for the next world. He also speaks of the nine virgin priestesses of the island of Sena, opposite the Osismii (III.48), and of Ireland (III.53).

fuentes/corografia-mela/por_que_importa.texto: After Strabo (IV.4.5), it is one of the first texts to present Gallic human sacrifice as a thing of the past, a century after the conquest, and it adds more to Caesar about the druids than any other, with data that have no other confirmation. Mela writes from books, and his island of Sena belongs to the same world of wonders at the edges of the map.

fuentes/farsalia/resumen.texto: Unfinished epic poem, in ten books, on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey. In book I (392-465), when Caesar withdraws his troops from Gaul, Lucan lists the peoples who were freed, names the gods who were appeased with blood (the cruel Teutates, the horrible Esus, and Taranis, whose altar is no kinder than that of the Scythian Diana), and addresses the druids: only they know the gods, or only they are ignorant of them, and they teach that death is the middle of a long life. In book III (399-452) he describes the sacred grove of Massilia, with altars soaked in human blood, which Caesar ordered cut down.

fuentes/farsalia/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only ancient source that names Teutates, Esus and Taranis together, and for that reason it carries great weight in reconstructions of Gallic religion. But it is rhetorical poetry, written a century after Caesar by someone not known to have been acquainted with Gaul, and its grove at Massilia is a literary picture of horror; the Bern scholia that comment on it are later still.

fuentes/farsalia/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Edward Ridley at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/farsalia/leer.1.titulo.texto: Book I in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/apocolocintosis/titulo.texto: Apocolocyntosis (The Pumpkinification of the Divine Claudius)

fuentes/apocolocintosis/resumen.texto: Prose and verse satire on the death of the emperor Claudius and his arrival in heaven, where the gods reject him and send him to the underworld. Hercules does not understand what he says and takes him for a monster; the goddess Fever explains that he was born in Lugdunum, that he is a true Gaul and that, as befits a Gaul, “he took Rome” (6).

fuentes/apocolocintosis/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that Gallic origin was still a subject of mockery in first-century Rome, even for an emperor born in Lyon who had defended the admission of Gauls to the Senate. The attribution to Seneca is the traditional one and most scholars accept it, though it is not certain.

fuentes/apocolocintosis/leer.0.titulo.texto: Edition by W. H. D. Rouse, with Latin text and English translation

fuentes/historia-natural-plinio/resumen.texto: Encyclopedia in thirty-seven books on the cosmos, geography, animals, plants, medicine and metals, dedicated to Titus. On the Celts it recounts the mistletoe rite: on the sixth day of the moon, a druid dressed in white cuts it from the oak with a golden sickle, and two white bulls are sacrificed (XVI.249-251); the druids' “serpent's egg,” for carrying which Claudius had a Vocontian knight executed (XXIX.52-54); Tiberius's suppression of “his druids and that class of diviners and healers” (XXX.13); the Helvetian Helicon, who returned from Rome with figs, grapes and wine and aroused the Gauls' greed for Italy (XII.5); and the 1,192,000 enemies killed by Caesar, not counting the civil wars (VII.92).

fuentes/historia-natural-plinio/por_que_.texto: Many of these data appear only in Pliny, who took them from his reading and from what he heard in the provinces where he served; his interest lies in curiosity and in the condemnation of magic, which he associates with the druids. Caesar's figure, which Pliny presents as an injury done to the human race, is among the most cited and most disputed (Henige 1998).

fuentes/historia-natural-plinio/leer.0.t.texto: Book XVI, 95 (mistletoe), translation by Bostock and Riley (Perseus)

fuentes/historia-natural-plinio/leer.1.t.texto: Book XXX, 4 (the druids and their suppression under Tiberius; XXX.13 in modern numbering), translation by Bostock and Riley (Perseus)

fuentes/agricola-tacito/resumen.texto: Biography of Gnaeus Julius Agricola, Tacitus's father-in-law and governor of Britain between 77 and 84, with an ethnography of the island. Tacitus says that the Caledonians, red-haired and large-limbed, seem of German origin; the Silures, dark-skinned and curly-haired, of Iberian origin; and those of the south, similar to the Gauls in religion and language (11); that they fight from chariots and that their disunity made them prey to Rome (12); that Agricola lured them with baths, colonnades and banquets, “and the ignorant called civilization what was part of their servitude” (21); and he puts into the mouth of the Caledonian Calgacus, before Mount Graupius, the speech against Rome that says “they make a desert and call it peace” (30-32).

fuentes/agricola-tacito/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source for the conquest of northern Britain and the harshest criticism of Romanization written by a Roman. But Calgacus's speech is Tacitus's rhetorical invention, in which he uses the noble barbarian to criticize the Rome of Domitian, and the book is also an interested eulogy of his father-in-law.

fuentes/agricola-tacito/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Church and Brodribb, with the Germania

fuentes/germania-tacito/resumen.texto: Ethnography of the Germanic peoples. On the Celts it says that the Gauls were once more powerful and crossed the Rhine: the Helvetii occupied the land between the Hercynian Forest, the Rhine and the Main, and the Boii the land beyond, which is still called Boihaemum, Bohemia (28); that the Treveri and the Nervii boasted of a German origin so as not to resemble the Gauls (28); that the Cotini speak Gaulish and pay tribute (43); and that the language of the Aestii, on the Baltic, resembles that of the Britons (45).

fuentes/germania-tacito/por_que_importa.texto: After Strabo (VII.1.3) and Velleius Paterculus (II.109), it is one of the oldest sources for the name of Bohemia, and one of the few ancient texts that distinguish peoples by language. There is no evidence that Tacitus was ever in Germany, and he uses the Germans, like the Britons in the Agricola, to set barbarian simplicity against Roman vices.

fuentes/germania-tacito/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Church and Brodribb, with the Agricola

fuentes/historias-tacito/resumen.texto: History of the Empire from 69 to 96, of which books I to IV and part of V survive, covering the years 69 and 70. It tells of the revolt of the Boian Maricus, who proclaimed himself “liberator of the Gauls” and a god (II.61), and of the rebellion of the Batavian Civilis, which was joined by the Treveri and Lingones under Classicus, Tutor and Sabinus with their “Empire of the Gauls” (IV.12-79). It says that the druids announced that the burning of the Capitol in 69 was a sign that dominion of the world would pass to the peoples beyond the Alps (IV.54), and it puts into the mouth of the general Cerialis, at Trier, the justification of Roman rule: without Rome the Gauls would have kings and wars, and there is no peace without armies or armies without tribute (IV.73-74).

fuentes/historias-tacito/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only source for the last Gallic revolt with aspirations to independence, and for the persistence of the druids more than a century after Caesar. Tacitus writes from the Roman side, but he gives voice to the rebels and to Rome with the same irony.

fuentes/historias-tacito/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book IV, 54 (the druids' prophecy), translation by Church and Brodribb (Perseus)

fuentes/historias-tacito/leer.1.titulo.texto: Book IV in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/vidas-de-los-doce-cesares/resume.texto: Biographies of Caesar and of the eleven emperors who followed, up to Domitian. On the Gauls it recounts that Caesar plundered sanctuaries and temples full of offerings and destroyed cities more for booty than for punishment (Julius 54); that verses circulated in Rome mocking the fact that Caesar had led the Gauls in his triumph and then into the Senate (Julius 80); that Caligula disguised tall Gauls as Germans for a sham triumph (Caligula 47); and that Augustus forbade Druidism to Roman citizens and Claudius abolished it altogether for its “cruel inhumanity” (Claudius 25.5).

fuentes/vidas-de-los-doce-cesares/por_qu.texto: Together with Pliny, it is the main source for the prohibition of Druidism, and one of the few Roman texts that records Caesar's plundering of Gallic temples. Suetonius gathers rumors and jokes of the time with little filtering.

fuentes/vidas-de-los-doce-cesares/leer.1.texto: Life of Claudius in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/epitome-de-floro/resumen.texto: Summary in two books of Rome's wars from Romulus to Augustus, based mainly on Livy and presented as the ages of a single person. In book I it covers the Gallic sack of Rome, the wars with the Insubres, whose leaders had promised their gods Roman arms or booty, the Cimbri and Teutones, Numantia and Viriathus, and the conquest of Gaul, which ends with Vercingetorix throwing his weapons at Caesar's feet and saying that he was handing a brave man over to the bravest, who had defeated him.

fuentes/epitome-de-floro/por_que_importa.texto: It was a widely read school text in the Middle Ages and fixed famous scenes, such as Vercingetorix's surrender, which is not in Caesar. Florus adds rhetorical color and phrases invented for Livy, and he is not an independent source.

fuentes/estratagemas-polieno/resumen.texto: Collection in eight books of about nine hundred military and political stratagems, dedicated to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus for the war against the Parthians (162-166). Book VII gathers those of barbarian kings and peoples, among them several involving Celts and Galatians, and Book VIII those of Romans and of women, among them that of the Galatian Camma, who poisoned at her wedding the murderer of her husband.

fuentes/estratagemas-polieno/por_que_imp.texto: It preserves versions of Celtic episodes taken from lost historians, but without citing or criticizing them: it serves to trace traditions, not to date them.

fuentes/estratagemas-polieno/leer.0.titu.texto: Book VII in the English translation by R. Shepherd (1793), at attalus.org

fuentes/estratagemas-polieno/leer.1.titu.texto: Book VIII (with Camma) in Shepherd's translation, at attalus.org

fuentes/epigramas-marcial/resumen.texto: Twelve books of epigrams, plus the Xenia and Apophoreta, on daily life in Rome. In several places Martial presents himself as a Spaniard from Bilbilis: he proclaims himself “born of Celts and Iberians” and is not ashamed of the “rough” names of the Celtiberian places, which he lists in verse (IV.55); he sets himself against an effeminate Greek as a virile Celtiberian (X.65); and in the preface to book XII, written back in Bilbilis, he misses the Roman public.

fuentes/epigramas-marcial/por_que_import.texto: He is one of the few ancient authors who called themselves Celtic, and it shows that in the first century that identity could be a provincial pride within Latin culture. His Celtiberism is rhetorical: it contrasts the roughness of his land with Greek refinement.

fuentes/coleccion-de-cosas-memorables/re.texto: Compendium of geographical curiosities, arranged by region and taken for the most part from Pliny and Mela. He adds about Ireland that there are no snakes or bees and that, after victory, the warriors drink the blood of the dead and smear their faces with it; and about Britain, that in the sanctuary of the hot springs (Bath) Minerva was worshipped with fires that were never extinguished (22).

fuentes/coleccion-de-cosas-memorables/po.texto: His additions about Ireland, which have no known source, fed for centuries the image of the Irish as savages; it was widely read in the Middle Ages. The Bath detail matches the sanctuary of Sulis Minerva known from archaeology.

fuentes/historia-augusta/resumen.texto: Collection of biographies of emperors from Hadrian to Carinus (117-285), which claims to have been written by six authors of the time of Diocletian and Constantine. It recounts three prophecies by druidesses: one warned Severus Alexander, in Gaulish, not to expect victory or trust his soldiers (Severus Alexander 60.6); another predicted to Diocletian, when he was a soldier at Tongeren, that he would become emperor when he killed a boar (Numerian 14); and Aurelian consulted Gallic druidesses about the future of his descendants (Aurelian 44.4).

fuentes/historia-augusta/por_que_importa.texto: They are the only ancient mentions of women druids. But since Dessau (1889) it has generally been accepted that the work is by a single author of the late fourth century who invents documents, names and anecdotes, so these druidesses may be literary invention; at most they show that by then the word evoked Gallic female seers.

fuentes/instituciones-divinas/resumen.texto: The first systematic exposition of Christianity in Latin, in seven books, addressed to educated pagans. In book I (21), speaking of the human sacrifices of pagan peoples, he says that the Gauls appeased Esus and Teutates with human blood.

fuentes/instituciones-divinas/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the few mentions of Gallic gods outside Lucan, from whom he probably takes it, and he uses it as an argument against pagan religion, not as information.

fuentes/instituciones-divinas/leer.0.tit.texto: Book I, English translation of the Ante-Nicene Fathers (New Advent)

fuentes/res-gestae-amiano/resumen.texto: History of the Empire in thirty-one books, from Nerva to the battle of Adrianople (378), of which books XIV to XXXI survive. In the excursus on Gaul (XV.9-12) he records, according to Timagenes, several versions of its origin (native inhabitants, Dorians who followed Heracles, fugitive Trojans) and what the druids said: that part of the population was native and part came from distant islands and from beyond the Rhine (XV.9.4). He describes bards, euhages (vates) and druids, the last “united in communities, as the authority of Pythagoras commanded” (XV.9.8), and the Gauls of his own time: tall, fair-haired and clean (no one is seen dirty and in rags, however poor), fit for war at any age, and with women stronger than their husbands (XV.12).

fuentes/res-gestae-amiano/por_que_import.texto: It is the only ethnography of the Gauls written by someone who dealt with them in person in the late Empire, but it mixes what was seen in the fourth century with what was copied from Timagenes three centuries earlier. Through Timagenes it preserves the only tradition about the origin of the Gauls attributed to the druids themselves.

fuentes/res-gestae-amiano/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by C. D. Yonge at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/res-gestae-amiano/leer.1.titulo.texto: Book XV in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/conmemoracion-de-los-profesores-.texto: Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux

Series of short poems in memory of the teachers of grammar and rhetoric whom Ausonius knew in Bordeaux. Two of them speak of Gallic religious lineages: the rhetorician Attius Patera, of Bayeux, “descendant of druids,” whose family served in the temple of Belenus and whose name came from the priests of Apollo (IV), and the grammarian Phoebicius, guardian of the temple of Belenus, also of druidic stock, from Armorica (X).

It shows that in fourth-century Gaul some families of the educated elite proudly remembered a druidic origin and a cult of Belenus. It does not say they practiced Druidism: it presents it as a prestigious genealogy, assimilated to Apollo.
Works of Ausonius in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/ora-maritima/resumen.texto: Geographical poem, of which about seven hundred lines survive, describing the coasts from Britain and the Oestrymnides islands to Massilia. He says he follows ancient sources, among them the periplus of the Carthaginian Himilco; he mentions the “sacred island” of the Hiernians (Ireland) near that of the Albiones (Britain); he says that the Celts drove the Ligurians out of their northern lands; and he describes the Tartessians, the Cempsi and the Sefes of the peninsula.

fuentes/ora-maritima/por_que_importa.texto: Since Schulten (1922) it has been believed that it reworks a sixth-century BC Massaliot periplus, which would make it the oldest testimony of the Celts in the Atlantic and of the names of Ireland and Britain. Many scholars reject that date: the text mixes layers from different periods, and Avienus may have combined Hellenistic sources, so its data cannot be dated with certainty.

fuentes/historias-contra-los-paganos/res.texto: Universal history in seven books, from Adam to 417, written at the request of Augustine of Hippo to show that before Christ the world had suffered worse calamities than the sack of Rome in 410. He compares the Gallic sack of Rome with that of Alaric (II.19); he recounts that after defeating the Cimbri at Arausio, the Romans destroyed all the booty, threw the gold and silver into the river, drowned the horses and hanged the prisoners from trees (V.16); and he summarizes Caesar's Gallic War (VI.7-12). In his description of the world (I.2) he places the Galician city of Brigantia, with its lighthouse, opposite Britain and Ireland.

fuentes/historias-contra-los-paganos/por.texto: It was the ancient history textbook of the Middle Ages, and through it these episodes became known in the West. Its apologetic aim leads him to stress pagan massacres; for the Gauls he copies Livy, Caesar, Justin and Florus, and contributes only information specific to his native Gallaecia.

fuentes/vida-de-san-martin/resumen.texto: Biography of Martin, a soldier turned monk and bishop of Tours, written while he was still alive. It tells how Martin roamed the Gallic countryside destroying temples and sacred trees; with the sign of the cross he stopped a venerated pine that peasants were about to bring down on him (13); he halted a funeral procession that he took for a pagan one, because Gallic peasants used to parade through their fields images covered with white veils (12); and he built churches on the spots where he destroyed sanctuaries (13-15).

fuentes/vida-de-san-martin/por_que_impor.texto: It is the key text on the Christianization of rural Gaul and one of the few descriptions of peasant cults from the fourth century. It is hagiography: the miracles and the pagan resistance magnify the saint, and it does not say which gods were worshipped.

fuentes/vida-de-san-martin/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by A. Roberts (New Advent)

fuentes/vida-de-san-martin/leer.1.titulo.texto: Works of Sulpicius Severus in Latin (The Latin Library)

fuentes/de-medicamentis/resumen.texto: Medical recipe book in Latin that gathers remedies from earlier authors and from popular Gallic medicine, with plants, amulets and incantations. Some incantations against diseases of the eyes, the throat or the stomach contain words in Gaulish, or in a mixture of Gaulish and Latin, and Gaulish names of plants.

fuentes/de-medicamentis/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the last written sources to preserve phrases in Gaulish, which are very hard to interpret, and it documents popular magical practices in Christian Gaul. The Gaulish reading of many of the formulas is disputed.

fuentes/cartas-de-sidonio-apolinar/resum.texto: Nine books of letters to friends and relatives of the Gallo-Roman aristocracy, in a highly elaborate Latin, about the life of their class, the Church, and the arrival of the Visigoths and Burgundians. In a letter to his brother-in-law Ecdicius (III.3) he thanks him for the fact that the Arvernian nobility, thanks to him, has shed “the crust of the Celtic speech” in order to learn Latin rhetoric and poetry.

fuentes/cartas-de-sidonio-apolinar/por_q.texto: It is one of the last testimonies to spoken Gaulish, in Auvergne around 470. It is debated whether it refers to the Gaulish language or, figuratively, to rustic speech; if it is literal, it would show that Gaulish still survived among the nobility of central Gaul.

fuentes/cartas-de-sidonio-apolinar/leer..texto: Book III in the English translation by O. M. Dalton (1915)

fuentes/epistola-a-los-galatas/resumen.texto: Letter from Paul to the Christian communities “of Galatia,” whom he rebukes for having accepted preachers who demanded circumcision and the law of Moses: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” (3:1). He argues that faith in Christ is enough, that in him “there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female” (3:28), and recalls that the Galatians received him as an angel when he arrived sick (4:13-14).

fuentes/epistola-a-los-galatas/por_que_i.texto: It is the oldest text addressed to communities in a region where Celtic was partly spoken, though it says nothing about their language or origin. It is debated whether the addressees were the northern Galatians (Ancyra, Pessinus, Tavium) or the cities of the southern part of the province of Galatia (Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra), which Paul visited according to Acts and which were not Celtic; Jerome read them as Celts.

fuentes/epistola-a-los-galatas/leer.1.ti.texto: Greek, Latin and English text (New Advent)

fuentes/comentario-a-galatas-jeronimo/ti.texto: Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians

fuentes/comentario-a-galatas-jeronimo/re.texto: Commentary in three books on Paul's letter, written in Bethlehem around 386-387. In the prologue to book II, to explain to whom Paul was writing, Jerome summarizes what he knew about the Galatians: that they were Gauls who had come to Asia, that according to Lactantius their name came from the whiteness of their skin, and that, besides the Greek spoken throughout the East, they had their own language, “almost the same as that of the Treveri.”

fuentes/comentario-a-galatas-jeronimo/po.texto: It is the most cited testimony that Galatian was still spoken in the fourth century, and of its kinship with the Gaulish of the Trier region, where Jerome had lived as a young man. Some scholars doubt that he could compare the two languages and think he repeats a datum from his reading; others accept it as his own observation, though imprecise.

fuentes/denario-de-hostilio-saserna/titu.texto: Denarius of Lucius Hostilius Saserna with the head of a Gaul

fuentes/denario-de-hostilio-saserna/resu.texto: Denarius minted in Rome in 48 BC by the moneyer Lucius Hostilius Saserna, in the midst of the civil war, celebrating Caesar's victories in Gaul. The obverse shows the head of a Gaul with long, tousled hair and a beard, with a Gallic shield behind; the reverse, a Gallic war chariot with a charioteer and a warrior brandishing a spear. Another issue by the same moneyer bears a female head with a Gallic war trumpet (carnyx), interpreted as Gaul itself.

fuentes/denario-de-hostilio-saserna/por_.texto: It is one of the few Roman images of a Gaul made during the lifetime of the principals. Since the nineteenth century it has been repeated that it portrays Vercingetorix, held prisoner in Rome in those years, but many numismatists read it as a generic Gaul, equipped with the features of the barbarian stereotype.

fuentes/denario-de-hostilio-saserna/leer.texto: Photographs of its coins on Wikimedia Commons

fuentes/denario-trofeo-galo-de-cesar/tit.texto: Denarius of Caesar with a Gallic trophy and two captives

fuentes/denario-trofeo-galo-de-cesar/res.texto: Denarius minted by order of Caesar in 46-45 BC, probably in Hispania during the war against the Pompeians. The obverse shows the head of Venus, from whom Caesar claimed descent; the reverse, a trophy of Gallic arms with two seated captives at its foot, a woman in mourning and a bearded man with his hands tied behind his back, and the name CAESAR.

fuentes/denario-trofeo-galo-de-cesar/por.texto: It is the image of the conquest that the victor himself circulated among his soldiers, years after Alesia: Gaul as a pair of captives at the foot of their weapons. It is not a portrait but the generic figure of the vanquished, the same one repeated on the arches of Orange and Carpentras.

fuentes/galata-moribundo/soporte.texto: Marble sculpture, Roman copy of a lost bronze (Capitoline Museums)

fuentes/galata-moribundo/resumen.texto: Statue of a Galatian warrior mortally wounded, nude, seated on his shield, with a torc around his neck, a moustache and his hair stiffened into locks, beside a war trumpet. It is a Roman marble copy, from the first or second century, of a lost original, probably a bronze from the monument that Attalus I of Pergamon dedicated around 230-220 BC to celebrate his victories over the Galatians; that attribution is the most accepted hypothesis, but it is not documented, and some specialists propose that the group was created in Rome at the end of the Republic. It appeared in Rome at the beginning of the seventeenth century, and until the nineteenth it was called “the Dying Gladiator.”

fuentes/galata-moribundo/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most famous ancient image of a Celt, and it brings together the features that the texts describe: nudity in combat, the torc, the moustache and hair washed with lime (Diodorus V.28). It shows the vanquished with dignity in order to exalt the victor: it is not a portrait but a type, and the nudity may be a Greek heroic convention as much as a Gallic custom.

fuentes/galata-ludovisi/soporte.texto: Marble sculpture, Roman copy (Palazzo Altemps, Rome)

fuentes/galata-ludovisi/resumen.texto: Sculptural group of a Galatian warrior who holds up the body of his wife, whom he has just killed, and runs his sword into his own chest so as not to fall captive. It is a Roman marble copy of a lost original, usually attributed to the same Pergamene group as the Dying Galatian, with the same doubts about its date and origin.

fuentes/galata-ludovisi/por_que_importa.texto: It represents the defeated rather than the victor, with a dramatism that makes Gallic defeat a noble theme. It spread the image of the proud barbarian who prefers death, which also appears in the texts on the retreat from Delphi (Pausanias X.23, Justin XXIV.8).

fuentes/arco-de-orange/resumen.texto: Three-bay triumphal arch at the entrance to the Roman colony of Arausio (Orange), in Narbonensis, whose date is debated: current research places it in the time of Augustus, and an inscription dedicated it to Tiberius in 26-27. Its reliefs show battles between Romans and Gauls, Gauls in chains beside trophies of arms and naval spoils; some shields bear Gallic names, such as Boduacus and Sacrovir.

fuentes/arco-de-orange/por_que_importa.texto: It is the largest program of images of the defeated Gaul that survives in Gaul itself, erected for the veteran colonists and for the Gauls of the province. It is debated whether the names on the shields refer to real chieftains (Sacrovir led the revolt of 21) or are signatures or conventional names.

fuentes/arco-de-carpentras/resumen.texto: Single-bay Roman arch, from the early first century, at Carpentorate (Carpentras), in Narbonensis. On its sides it has reliefs of trophies of arms with barbarian prisoners in chains, like those on the short sides of the arch of Orange, which are usually read as captives from the north and from the East.

fuentes/arco-de-carpentras/por_que_impor.texto: It shows the Roman formula of the captive beside the trophy, repeated on coins and monuments, in a city of the Gallic province: the vanquished from every edge of the Empire, interchangeable in propaganda.

fuentes/relieve-de-claudio-y-britania/ti.texto: Relief of Claudius Conquering Britain (Sebasteion of Aphrodisias)

fuentes/relieve-de-claudio-y-britania/re.texto: Relief from the Sebasteion, the sanctuary of the imperial cult at Aphrodisias, in Caria, built in the mid-first century. It shows the emperor Claudius, nude like a hero, about to strike a fallen woman who represents Britain; it forms part of a series with the peoples subjected by Rome and of another with Nero dominating Armenia.

fuentes/relieve-de-claudio-y-britania/po.texto: It is the rawest image of the conquest of a Celtic people, represented as violence against a woman, made in Asia Minor for a Greek audience. It shows that the propaganda of the conquest of Britain reached the whole Empire.

fuentes/relieve-de-claudio-y-britania/le.texto: Photographs of the Sebasteion on Wikimedia Commons

fuentes/celtic-ethnography-of-posidonius.texto: Article (Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy 60C, 189-275)

Study that gathered and translated the passages from Athenaeus, Diodorus, Strabo and Caesar that, according to the author, derive from the lost Histories of Posidonius, and presented them as a single coherent ethnography of the Celts around 100 BC. He argued that Caesar took much of his excursus on Gaul (BG VI.11-28), especially what he says about the druids, from Posidonius instead of describing what he saw.

For decades it was the basis of many books on the Celts, which cite its collection as if it were the text of Posidonius. Nash (1976) criticized the method, which attributes to Posidonius everything that resembles him and denies Caesar any information of his own, and the editions of Theiler (1982) and of Edelstein and Kidd show how different the division of material among lost authors can be.

fuentes/reconstructing-poseidonios-nash/.texto: Reconstructing Poseidonios' Celtic Ethnography: Some Considerations

Response to Tierney. Nash points out that Posidonius is known only through derivative authors, that almost all the attributions are inferences without citation, that two authors who say the same thing do not necessarily copy the same source, and that attributions slide from the certain to the doubtful. Nash concludes that there is no evidence that Caesar plagiarized Posidonius, that his information came from his long experience in Gaul, and that the two described different Celts at different moments: the agreements may be real and lasting traits, such as clientship, and the differences historical changes.

It recovered Caesar as a source on the Gaul of his time, and it is the starting point of modern criticism of ancient ethnography. Its weakest point is assuming that traits repeated in several authors are lasting realities: studies of ancient ethnography as a genre (Woolf 2011) show that topoi were also inherited from one author to another.

fuentes/posidonius-fragments-edelstein-k.texto: Posidonius: The Fragments, The Commentary, The Translation of the Fragments
Ludwig Edelstein and Ian G. Kidd
Greek and Latin, with commentary in English

Edition of the fragments of Posidonius (1972), with Kidd's commentary (1988) and his translation (1999). It admits as fragments only passages in which an ancient author names Posidonius, so that his ethnography of the Celts is reduced to the quotations from Athenaeus and Strabo, and it leaves out the chapters of Diodorus V that others attribute to him.

It is the reference edition and the strict criterion opposed to Tierney's. Theiler's edition (1982), which is broader, includes many passages attributed by inference: the difference between the two shows how much of the portrait of the Celts depends on how the material is divided among lost authors.

fuentes/celts-and-the-classical-world/re.texto: Survey of what Greeks and Romans wrote about the Celts, author by author and theme by theme: the first geographers, the invasion of Greece, the Galatians, the Gaul of Posidonius and Caesar, the druids, women, religion and language. Rankin, a Hellenist, reads the texts as evidence of a cultural encounter and seeks behind the topoi real features of Celtic society, sometimes with Irish parallels.

fuentes/celts-and-the-classical-world/po.texto: It is the most complete single-volume guide to the classical sources on the Celts. Its premise of a common Celtic culture, from the continent to Ireland, which authorizes those parallels, is the one discussed by the Celtic skeptics (James 1999, Collis 2003), and some of its readings of the texts are speculative.

fuentes/war-women-and-druids/titulo.texto: War, Women, and Druids: Eyewitness Reports and Early Accounts of the Ancient Celts

fuentes/war-women-and-druids/resumen.texto: Anthology of English translations of the main Greek and Latin passages on the Celts, from Hecataeus to the authors of the late Empire, arranged by author and with brief introductions.

fuentes/war-women-and-druids/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most practical collection of the classical texts. Its title speaks of “eyewitness” accounts, but almost none of the authors was one, and the selection, without critical apparatus, can give a sense of direct testimony that the texts do not have.

fuentes/the-philosopher-and-the-druids/t.texto: The Philosopher and the Druids: A Journey Among the Ancient Celts

fuentes/the-philosopher-and-the-druids/r.texto: Popular book that reconstructs Posidonius's journey to Gaul around 100 BC and, from it, presents the society, war, religion and druids of the Celts according to the classical sources and archaeology.

fuentes/the-philosopher-and-the-druids/p.texto: It is the most accessible presentation of Posidonius's ethnography. But it narrates with imagined details a journey of which no direct account survives, and it follows the broad attribution of Tierney that Nash and Kidd discuss.

fuentes/the-celtic-heroic-age/titulo.texto: The Celtic Heroic Age: Literary Sources for Ancient Celtic Europe and Early Ireland and Wales

fuentes/the-celtic-heroic-age/soporte.texto: Anthology edited with John Carey (Celtic Studies Publications; 4th ed., 2003)

fuentes/the-celtic-heroic-age/resumen.texto: Anthology edited by John T. Koch with the collaboration of John Carey, with translations of Greek and Latin texts on the ancient Celts, of inscriptions in continental Celtic languages, and of medieval Irish and Welsh texts (sagas, laws, poems), with introductions and notes.

fuentes/the-celtic-heroic-age/por_que_im.texto: It is the most widely used reference work for reading the classical testimonies together with texts in Celtic languages. Gathering them under a common “Celtic heroic age” implies a continuity between ancient Gaul and medieval Ireland that anti-nativists (McCone 1990) and the Celtic skeptics dispute.

fuentes/extraordinary-voyage-of-pytheas/.texto: The Extraordinary Voyage of Pytheas the Greek

Reconstruction of Pytheas's voyage from the fragments and from the archaeology of the Atlantic coasts in the fourth century BC: the route to Armorica, the return to Britain, the tin mines of Cornwall and the search for Thule.

It places Pytheas in the archaeological context of the Atlantic Iron Age. Many stages of the voyage are conjectures based on scant fragments, and his idea of a common Atlantic world is the same one that Cunliffe maintains in his theses on the western origin of the Celts, theses that other specialists discuss.

fuentes/pytheas-on-the-ocean-roseman/tit.texto: Pytheas of Massalia: On the Ocean

fuentes/pytheas-on-the-ocean-roseman/sop.texto: Edition with translation and commentary (Ares Publishers)

fuentes/pytheas-on-the-ocean-roseman/res.texto: Edition of the fragments and testimonies on Pytheas, with the Greek or Latin text, an English translation and a commentary on each passage.

fuentes/pytheas-on-the-ocean-roseman/por.texto: It is the reference edition in English, alongside the Italian edition by Serena Bianchetti (1998), and it allows one to separate what the fragments say from what their ancient critics and modern reconstructors add. It does not resolve, because the fragments do not suffice, the doubts about the route and about where Thule was.

fuentes/tales-of-the-barbarians/titulo.texto: Tales of the Barbarians: Ethnography and Empire in the Roman West

fuentes/tales-of-the-barbarians/resumen.texto: Study of how the Romans wrote about the peoples of the conquered West. Woolf argues that ancient ethnography was not fieldwork but a literary genre of origin myths and topoi, which persisted even when conquest brought better information, and that the provincials themselves, such as Romanized Gauls, adopted it to tell their past on a middle ground between conquerors and conquered.

fuentes/tales-of-the-barbarians/por_que_.texto: It explains why the texts repeat the same topoi for centuries and why they cannot be read as observation. It is a brief essay, born from a series of lectures, which chooses examples and does not go through all the sources.

fuentes/beyond-the-rubicon/titulo.texto: Beyond the Rubicon: Romans and Gauls in Republican Italy

fuentes/beyond-the-rubicon/resumen.texto: Study of how the Romans built the image of the Gauls of Italy, from the sack of Rome to Caesar. Williams argues that the “Gauls” of the texts are to a large extent a literary and political category, made from Greek topoi and Roman memory, which served to shape northern Italy as a frontier and to justify its conquest.

fuentes/beyond-the-rubicon/por_que_impor.texto: It is a central study of the Roman fear of the Gauls as a construction. Its reading is disputed because the archaeology of La Tène in Cisalpine Gaul and the Gaulish and Lepontic inscriptions document real Celtic populations, which the literary approach tends to push into the background.

fuentes/caesar-in-gaul-and-rome/titulo.texto: Caesar in Gaul and Rome: War in Words

fuentes/caesar-in-gaul-and-rome/resumen.texto: Analysis of Caesar's Commentaries as a political text addressed to the Roman public. Riggsby argues that Caesar constructs Gauls and Germans using the molds of Greek ethnography in order to present the conquest as defense, that through them he defines Roman virtue and his own, and that the apparently neutral, third-person style serves persuasion.

fuentes/caesar-in-gaul-and-rome/por_que_.texto: It is one of the most cited readings of the Gallic War as a persuasive text. Unlike Rambaud (1953), who looked for the distortions of the facts, it is less interested in whether Caesar lies than in what image of Rome he constructs. It concentrates on the text and does not check it against archaeology or figures, which others handle (Henige 1998).

fuentes/tetrabiblos/resumen.texto: Treatise on astrology in four books, written by Ptolemy after the Almagest. In Book II (ch. 3) he distributes the peoples of the inhabited world among the signs of the zodiac and the planets that rule them: Britain, Gaul, Germany and Bastarnia, in the northwest, would have an affinity with Aries and Mars, and that is why their inhabitants would generally be fiercer, more obstinate and bestial; the northwestern quarter is 'independent, lover of freedom and fond of arms'.
