fuentes/tetrabiblos/por_que_importa.texto: It is an ethnographic passage, not an observation: it applies the astrological scheme of climes and the characters of peoples to the Celts and Germans of the north, and repeats the ancient commonplace of the warlike and untamed northerner. It gives no data of its own about any people.

personas/hecateo-de-mileto/resumen.texto: Ionian geographer and historian, author of a Journey Around the Earth (Periegesis) and of Genealogies of which only fragments survive, quoted by later authors. He is the first known author to name the Celts, in three entries preserved by Stephanus of Byzantium: he places Massalia “next to Celtica” and calls Narbo and the city of Nyrax Celtic, although it is not certain that the adjective is his and not that of the person who summarized him. He traveled through Egypt and Asia, but there is no sign that he knew the western Mediterranean; his information probably came from the navigators of Phocaea and Massalia.

personas/piteas/resumen.texto: Greek navigator and astronomer of Massalia who around 325 BC traveled through the Atlantic to Britain and farther north, and recounted it in On the Ocean. He is the first to describe the Pretannic Islands, the tin of Belerion (Cornwall) and the distant Thule. His work was lost, and we know it through Strabo, who calls him a liar following Polybius, through Pliny and, without naming him, probably through Diodorus; modern criticism confirms many of his astronomical data.

personas/eforo/resumen.texto: Greek historian from Cyme, in Aeolis, author of the first Greek universal history, in thirty books, now lost. Through Strabo we know that he counted the Celts among the four great peoples at the ends of the world, that he extended Celtica as far as Gades, and that he described them as friends of the Greeks. He wrote from books and informants, without traveling to the west.

personas/timeo-de-tauromenio/resumen.texto: Greek historian of Sicily who, exiled by the tyrant Agathocles, lived some fifty years in Athens and wrote a history of Sicily and of the West, now lost. Diodorus, Pliny and others take from him information on the Celts, Britain, tin and amber. Polybius devoted his book XII to accusing him of writing from the library, without having seen the places.

personas/jenofonte/resumen.texto: Athenian historian and soldier, disciple of Socrates, who led the Ten Thousand across Asia (Anabasis) and wrote the Hellenica, a continuation of Thucydides. In it he records the arrival in the Peloponnese, in 369 BC, of Celtic and Iberian mercenaries sent by Dionysius I of Syracuse to aid Sparta: one of the first reports of Celts in Greece, written by a contemporary.

personas/calimaco/resumen.texto: Greek poet and scholar from Cyrene who worked in the library of Alexandria under Ptolemy II, for which he compiled the Pinakes, the first catalogue of Greek literature. In the Hymn to Delos he presents the Galatians who attacked Delphi as “late Titans” and celebrates the victory of Ptolemy II over his rebellious Galatian mercenaries: court poetry that turns a political event into myth.

personas/apolonio-de-rodas/resumen.texto: Poet and librarian of Alexandria, author of the Argonautica. In book IV he takes the Argonauts through the rivers and lakes of the Celts and records a Celtic legend about amber as the tears of Apollo: the land of the Celts as the mythical edge of the known world.

personas/polibio/resumen.texto: Achaean political and military leader from Megalopolis, taken to Rome as a hostage in 167 BC, where he became a friend and adviser of Scipio Aemilianus, whom he accompanied at the destruction of Carthage (146 BC) and probably at Numantia (133 BC). His Histories explain how Rome came to dominate the world, and treat the wars with the Gauls of Italy as a stage in that rise. He knew a great deal first-hand: he crossed the Alps following the route of Hannibal, spoke with witnesses and met the Galatian Chiomara at Sardis. His outlook is that of an ally of the Roman aristocracy, and he explains Gallic defeats by a character guided by impulse rather than by reason.

personas/posidonio/resumen.texto: Stoic philosopher from Apamea in Syria who taught in Rhodes, where Cicero and Pompey visited him, and wrote Histories continuing Polybius, now lost. Around 100 BC he traveled through Hispania (he observed the tides at Gades), Liguria and southern Gaul, and saw severed heads nailed to the doors of houses. What remains of his ethnography of the Celts consists of quotations from Athenaeus and Strabo, and it is probably the source, without naming it, of much of Diodorus V and Strabo IV, although how much may be attributed to him is disputed (Tierney 1960, Nash 1976). As a Stoic, he saw in “primitive” peoples earlier stages of humanity, and that idea colors what he describes.

personas/ciceron/resumen.texto: Roman orator, lawyer and politician, consul in 63 BC, whose speeches, treatises and letters are the richest source on Rome in his time. He speaks of the Gauls as a lawyer and as a politician: in Pro Fonteio (69 BC) he portrays them as barbarians without respect for oaths in order to discredit the Gallic witnesses, and in On Divination (44 BC) he has his brother Quintus recall the Aeduan druid Diviciacus, who had been Cicero's guest. His brother Quintus was Caesar's legate in Gaul and in Britain, and sent him news from the front. He was murdered on the orders of Mark Antony.

personas/aulo-hircio/resumen.texto: Officer and secretary of Caesar, consul in 43 BC, who died that year in the battle of Mutina against Mark Antony. He wrote book VIII of the Gallic War, covering the years 51 and 50 BC, and probably the Alexandrian War. He knew the war from Caesar's general staff and writes to defend his memory.

personas/timagenes/resumen.texto: Greek rhetorician and historian from Alexandria, captured in 55 BC and taken to Rome, where he was freed, taught rhetoric and frequented Augustus until they fell out and he burned his own writings. He wrote a universal history and, according to Ammianus, gathered from many books what was known about the origins of the Gauls. That lost work is the source of Ammianus's excursus (XV.9); Strabo cites him on the gold of Tolosa, and some scholars believe that Pompeius Trogus also followed him.

personas/pompeyo-trogo/resumen.texto: Roman historian of Gallic origin, of the Vocontii people: his grandfather received Roman citizenship from Pompey during the war against Sertorius, and his father was secretary to Caesar. In the time of Augustus he wrote the Philippic Histories in forty-four books, a universal history centered on Macedon and the Hellenistic kingdoms that treats in detail the Gallic migrations, the attack on Delphi and the founding of Massalia. It is lost, and we know it through Justin's epitome; he is one of the few ancient authors of Gallic origin known, but he writes in Latin and from a Greco-Roman viewpoint.

personas/justino/resumen.texto: Latin author about whom almost nothing is known, who made an epitome of the Philippic Histories of Pompeius Trogus; his date is disputed between the second and fourth centuries. His summary preserves what Trogus said about the Gauls, cut down and with a moralizing style of its own.

personas/valerio-maximo/resumen.texto: Roman writer from the time of Tiberius who gathered in nine books anecdotes of memorable sayings and deeds for use by orators. He tells that the Gauls lent money to be repaid in the next world, because of their belief in the immortality of the soul, and that the Cimbri and Celtiberians feasted in battle and mourned in sickness.

personas/seneca/resumen.texto: Stoic philosopher and politician born in Corduba, tutor and adviser to Nero, who forced him to commit suicide in 65. In the Apocolocyntosis, a satire on the death of Emperor Claudius that tradition attributes to him, he mocks Claudius for having been born in Lugdunum and calls him a Gaul: Gallic origin was still a source of ridicule in first-century Rome.

personas/pomponio-mela/resumen.texto: Roman geographer born in Tingentera, on the Bay of Algeciras, author of the Chorographia (c. 43-44), the oldest surviving geographical work in Latin. He writes from books, and his description of the druids repeats and expands Caesar with details that have no other confirmation.

personas/lucano/resumen.texto: Roman poet born in Corduba, nephew of Seneca, who wrote the Pharsalia on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey and was forced to commit suicide by Nero after the Pisonian conspiracy. His verses on the cruel gods of the Gauls (Teutates, Esus, Taranis), the druids and the sacred grove of Massalia are literature, not observation: there is no record that he was ever in Gaul.

personas/plinio-el-viejo/resumen.texto: Cavalry officer in Germania, procurator in several provinces (among them Hispania Tarraconensis and probably Gaul) and admiral of the fleet at Misenum, he died in the eruption of Vesuvius in 79. His Natural History is an encyclopedia built from reading, with some observations of his own from the provinces where he served. On the Celts he offers what no one else reports: mistletoe and the golden sickle, the “serpent’s egg,” the suppression of the druids under Tiberius, and the figure of 1,192,000 dead attributed to Caesar.

personas/dion-crisostomo/resumen.texto: Greek orator and philosopher from Prusa, in Bithynia, exiled by Domitian and later close to Trajan. In one of his discourses (the 49th) he holds up the druids as an example of philosophers who govern kings, alongside the Persian magi and the Brahmins. He uses them to defend the role of the philosopher in politics, not to describe the Celts.

personas/suetonio/resumen.texto: Roman biographer, secretary to Hadrian until he fell out of favor around 122, who wrote the Lives of the Twelve Caesars with access to the imperial archives. Through him we know that Augustus forbade druidism to Roman citizens and Claudius abolished it, and that Caesar plundered Gallic temples. He is more interested in the anecdotes and morals of each emperor than in the peoples.

personas/floro/resumen.texto: Latin historian and poet, probably African, of the time of Trajan and Hadrian, author of an Epitome of the Roman Wars based mainly on Livy. He presents Roman history as the life of a single person, with the Gauls as the enemy of its youth, and adds to Livy phrases and dramatic scenes.

personas/apiano/resumen.texto: Greek historian from Alexandria, lawyer in Rome and procurator under Antoninus Pius, who wrote a Roman History organized by peoples and wars. His book on Iberia is the main source for the Celtiberian and Lusitanian wars and for Numantia, and fragments survive of his book on the Gauls. He summarizes earlier authors, above all Polybius, and sometimes confuses dates and names.

personas/arriano/resumen.texto: Greek historian and soldier from Nicomedia, disciple of the philosopher Epictetus, consul and governor of Cappadocia (c. 131-137), where he checked the Alans. His Anabasis of Alexander follows mainly the memoirs of Ptolemy I and Aristobulus, witnesses of the campaign, and preserves Alexander’s meeting with the Celts on the Danube. In his Tactica he says that the Roman cavalry had adopted exercises and words from the Celts.

personas/claudio-ptolomeo/resumen.texto: Greek astronomer and geographer from Alexandria, author of the Almagest and the Geography. His Geography gives coordinates for thousands of places and names of peoples in Hispania, Gaul, Britain and Ireland, and is the oldest description of the interior of Ireland. He worked from itineraries and earlier works, above all that of Marinus of Tyre, and never saw those lands.

personas/pausanias/resumen.texto: Greek traveler and geographer from Asia Minor who, in the second half of the 2nd century, wrote the Description of Greece, a guide to its cities, sanctuaries and monuments. He saw the votive offerings at Delphi and Athens that commemorated the defeat of the Galatians in 279 BC, and he tells the invasion as a new war against the Persians, miracles included.

personas/polieno/resumen.texto: Macedonian rhetorician who lived in Rome and dedicated eight books of Stratagems to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus for their war against the Parthians. He gathers anecdotes of military deception by Greeks, Romans and barbarians, among them several about Celts and Galatians, taken from earlier authors without criticism.

personas/luciano-de-samosata/resumen.texto: Satirical writer from Syria who wrote in Greek and traveled the empire as a lecturer, including through Gaul, where he says he earned good money. He claims to have seen there a painting of the Celtic Heracles, Ogmios, which a Celt explained to him as an image of eloquence; in another speech he narrates Antiochus I’s victory over the Galatians thanks to elephants.

personas/ateneo/resumen.texto: Greek writer from Naucratis, in Egypt, who around the year 200 composed the Deipnosophistae, a long dinner-table conversation full of quotations from books now lost. Thanks to him, the passages of Posidonius on Celtic banquets, the Arvernian king Luernius and table duels survive, quoted almost word for word. He knew nothing of the Celts firsthand: he chose quotations about food, drink and luxury.

personas/clemente-de-alejandria/resumen.texto: Christian theologian trained in Greek philosophy, teacher in Alexandria until the persecution of 202. In the Stromata he holds that philosophy first flourished among the barbarians, and he places the druids of the Gauls alongside the Egyptian prophets, the Persian magi and the gymnosophists of India, to argue that the Greeks did not invent wisdom.

personas/dion-casio/resumen.texto: Roman senator of Greek origin, from Nicaea, twice consul and governor of Pannonia and Dalmatia, who wrote a Roman History in eighty books down to 229. He is the main source for Boudica’s revolt, to which he gives an invented speech, and for the campaigns of Septimius Severus in Caledonia. He calls the Germans “Celts” and the Gauls “Galatians,” which confuses anyone who reads him carelessly.

personas/hipolito-de-roma/resumen.texto: Christian presbyter and theologian in Rome, at odds with the bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus, and exiled to Sardinia, where he died around 235. In the Refutation of All Heresies, attributed to him, he summarizes the doctrine of the druids as a branch of Pythagoreanism taught by Zalmoxis, the Thracian slave of Pythagoras: a learned construction, not information about the druids of his time.

personas/eliano/resumen.texto: Roman rhetorician from Praeneste who wrote in Greek, author of the Varied Histories and On the Nature of Animals, collections of curiosities drawn from books. He repeats the commonplace, which goes back to Aristotle and Ephorus, of Celts who face the waves of the sea and do not flee from houses that collapse on them.

personas/diogenes-laercio/resumen.texto: Greek biographer of the 3rd century, of whom almost nothing is known, author of the Lives of Eminent Philosophers. In the prologue he records the opinion that philosophy began among the barbarians, among them the druids of the Celts, citing lost works attributed to Aristotle and Sotion, and rejects it.

personas/solino/resumen.texto: Latin grammarian of the 3rd or 4th century, author of a Collection of Memorable Things taken almost entirely from Pliny and Mela. He adds information about Ireland that is not in his models, such as that the victors drink the blood of the dead and smear their faces with it.

personas/lactancio/resumen.texto: Christian rhetorician from North Africa, teacher in Nicomedia under Diocletian and later tutor of Crispus, son of Constantine. In the Divine Institutes, to attack Roman religion, he recalls that the Gauls appeased Esus and Teutates with human blood, a detail that seems taken from Lucan.

personas/amiano-marcelino/resumen.texto: Greek officer, probably from Antioch, who served in Gaul under Ursicinus (355-357) and accompanied Julian to Persia, and afterwards wrote in Latin, in Rome, a history of the Empire down to 378. His excursus on the Gauls (XV.9-12) mixes what he saw in the 4th century with what he copies from Timagenes, of the 1st century BC, on the origins of the Gauls and the druids, without separating one from the other.

personas/avieno/resumen.texto: Roman poet and aristocrat of the 4th century, from Volsinii, proconsul of Africa and of Achaea, who put earlier Greek geographical works into Latin verse. His Ora maritima reworks a much older periplus of the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts, with information about Celts, Ligurians and Tartessians whose original date is disputed.

personas/ausonio/resumen.texto: Rhetoric teacher from Bordeaux, tutor of the emperor Gratian and consul in 379, author of Latin poems such as the Mosella. In the Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux he tells that some colleagues descended from families of druids and from servants of the temple of Belenus, and in another poem he gives the Gaulish name of the spring of Bordeaux, Divona.

personas/sulpicio-severo/resumen.texto: Aquitanian lawyer from a noble family who, after being widowed, withdrew to an ascetic life on his estate at Primuliacum and became a disciple and biographer of Martin of Tours. His Life of Saint Martin tells how Martin destroyed the temples and sacred trees of the Gallic peasants, and in his Dialogues (I.27) a Gaul apologizes for his rustic speech and another replies that he should speak “in Celtic or, if he prefers, in Gaulish,” as long as he speaks of Martin.

personas/orosio/resumen.texto: Presbyter of Gallaecia, probably from Braga, who at the request of Augustine of Hippo wrote around 417 the Histories against the Pagans, to show that before Christianity misfortunes had been worse. That is why he tells in detail of the Roman defeats against the Gauls and the Cimbri and of the massacres of the Gallic War. He copies from Livy, from Caesar (whom he confuses with Suetonius), from Justin and from Florus, and adds only data from his own land.

personas/marcelo-empirico/resumen.texto: High-ranking Gallo-Roman official from Bordeaux, Master of Offices to the emperor Theodosius I, who around 410 compiled in Latin the book On Medicines, with remedies from folk medicine. Some of his charms preserve Gaulish words, one of the last written traces of that language.

personas/sidonio-apolinar/resumen.texto: Gallo-Roman aristocrat from Lyon, prefect of Rome in 468 and bishop of Clermont from around 470, who defended the city against the Visigoths. In a letter he thanks his brother-in-law Ecdicius for the Arvernian nobility having stripped itself of “the crust of Celtic speech,” one of the last, disputed, testimonies that Gaulish was spoken in the 5th century.

personas/esteban-de-bizancio/resumen.texto: Greek grammarian from Constantinople, of the time of Justinian, author of the Ethnica, a dictionary of cities and peoples that has survived in abridged form. It preserves fragments of lost authors, among them those of Hecataeus of Miletus that name the Celts for the first time.

personas/marcial/resumen.texto: Latin poet born in Bilbilis, near present-day Calatayud, who lived in Rome from 64 to 98 and then returned to his homeland, where he died. In his Epigrams he presents himself proudly as “born of Celts and Iberians” and defends the “rough” names of the Celtiberian places: one of the few ancient voices of someone who calls himself a Celt, though he writes like a Roman.

hechos/primera-mencion-de-los-celtas/tit.texto: First written mentions of the Celts

hechos/primera-mencion-de-los-celtas/res.texto: Around 500 BC Hecataeus of Miletus calls Massalia “a city of Liguria, next to Celtica,” in a fragment that Stephanus of Byzantium preserved a thousand years later. About sixty years later Herodotus (II.33, IV.49) places the Celts beyond the Pillars of Heracles, neighbors of the Cynetes, who are the westernmost people of Europe, and makes the Danube rise in their land, near a city called Pyrene. Both reports are second-hand and show that the Greeks called the peoples of the distant west and of the interior of Europe Celts, without specifying their limits.

hechos/mercenarios-celtas-de-dionisio/ti.texto: Celtic mercenaries of Dionysius I fight in Greece

hechos/mercenarios-celtas-de-dionisio/re.texto: In 369 BC Dionysius I of Syracuse sent ships with Celts, Iberians and horsemen to aid Sparta. They fought the Thebans and their allies near Corinth and Sicyon with rapid cavalry charges, and the following year he sent a second force. Xenophon, a contemporary, records them in the Hellenica (VII.1.20-22 and 28), and Diodorus (XV.70) tells the same: it is the first testimony of Celts as mercenaries in the Greek world, a century before the great invasion.

hechos/embajada-celta-a-alejandro/titulo.texto: Embassy of the Celts to Alexander on the Danube

hechos/embajada-celta-a-alejandro/resume.texto: In 335 BC, during his campaign against the Triballi and the Getae, Alexander received on the Danube envoys of the Celts who lived near the Ionian Gulf (the Adriatic). According to Ptolemy I, a witness whom Strabo cites (VII.3.8) and whom Arrian generally follows (Anabasis I.4.6-8), when the king asked them what they feared most, expecting to hear that it was him, they answered that they feared only that the sky might fall on them. Alexander declared them friends and called them braggarts. It is the first direct encounter between Celts and Greeks recounted by a witness. The reading of the phrase as a Celtic oath (“may the sky fall on us if we break our word”), supported by much later Irish parallels, is disputed.

hechos/viaje-de-piteas/titulo.texto: Voyage of Pytheas in the North Atlantic

hechos/viaje-de-piteas/resumen.texto: Around 325 BC the Greek Pytheas left Massalia, either passed through the Strait of Gades or crossed Gaul by land, followed the Atlantic coast to Armorica, traveled through Britain, visited the tin mines of Belerion (Cornwall), and heard of or reached Thule, six days’ sail to the north. His book was lost, and we know it through Strabo, who called him a liar, through Pliny and, without naming him, probably through Diodorus. The latitude he measured for Massalia is almost exact. It is the first description of Britain and its inhabitants, although the exact route and the location of Thule remain under discussion (Roseman 1994, Cunliffe 2001).

hechos/viaje-de-posidonio-a-la-galia/tit.texto: Voyage of Posidonius to Hispania and Gaul

hechos/viaje-de-posidonio-a-la-galia/res.texto: Around 100 BC the philosopher Posidonius traveled west from Rhodes. He was in Gades, where he observed the sunset and the tides, and he toured the coast of Liguria and southern Gaul, probably based in Massalia. Strabo (IV.4.5) preserves his testimony that at first he was repelled to see enemy heads nailed to the doors of houses, and that in time he grew used to it. His account is the basis of Greek ethnography of the Gauls, but what he saw was above all southern Gaul, in contact with Rome for decades, and it is not known how far inland he went (Nash 1976).

hechos/juicio-de-fonteyo/titulo.texto: Trial of Marcus Fonteius for extortion in Gaul

hechos/juicio-de-fonteyo/resumen.texto: In 69 BC the Allobroges and the Volcae brought charges in Rome, before the extortion court, against Marcus Fonteius, who had governed Transalpine Gaul in the previous decade and had imposed tributes, requisitions and labor on them during the war against Sertorius. Cicero defended him by discrediting the Gallic witnesses, among them the Allobrogian Indutiomarus, as barbarians who do not respect oaths or the gods, who sacrifice human beings, and who once besieged the Capitol. The verdict is not known with certainty, but the speech shows how an ethnic stereotype served as an argument in a Roman court.

hechos/diviciaco-en-roma/titulo.texto: The druid Diviciacus asks the Senate for help

hechos/diviciaco-en-roma/resumen.texto: Around 61 BC the Aeduan Diviciacus traveled to Rome to ask the Senate for help against the Sequani and the German Ariovistus, and returned without obtaining it (Caesar, BG VI.12). He was a guest of Cicero, whose brother Quintus remembers him as a druid, a student of nature and a diviner (De divinatione I.90): he is the only druid with a known name, recorded by someone who dealt with him. Caesar, who was his ally for years, never calls him a druid, and the detail appears only in Cicero.

hechos/prohibicion-druidica-de-la-escrit.texto: The druids do not entrust their doctrine to writing

Caesar (BG VI.14) says that the pupils of the druids learn by heart a great number of verses, sometimes for twenty years, and that the druids do not consider it lawful to entrust that teaching to writing, although in nearly everything else, in public and private accounts, they use Greek letters. He adds that, in his view, they do so for two reasons: so that the doctrine is not divulged and so that the pupils do not neglect their memory. The rule is recorded only by Caesar, and the reasons are his own conjecture (the map point marks the country of the Carnutes, where, according to him, the druids gathered). The same Caesar found in the Helvetian camp tablets in Greek letters with the census of the emigrants (BG I.29); Strabo (IV.1.5) says that the Gauls wrote their contracts in Greek under the influence of Massalia, and Diodorus (V.28) that they threw letters to the dead onto the pyres. According to Caesar, the rule concerned the teaching of the druids, not writing in general. The Celts left inscriptions in the alphabet of northern Italy (Lepontic, from the 6th century BC), in Greek letters (Gaulish in Greek script), in the Iberian script (Celtiberian) and in Latin (Gaulish of the Roman period); coin legends, the Coligny calendar, curse tablets such as the one from Larzac and, in Ireland and Britain, stones inscribed in Ogham. What has not survived is a history or a literature written by them before Christian Ireland, and that is why almost everything we know of them from antiquity was written by others.

hechos/discurso-de-agripa-ii/titulo.texto: Agrippa II holds up the Gauls as an example to the Jews

hechos/discurso-de-agripa-ii/resumen.texto: In 66, before the Jewish revolt against Rome, King Agrippa II tried to dissuade the inhabitants of Jerusalem with a long speech that Josephus reproduces (The Jewish War II.16.4) and that is largely Josephus’s own composition. Among the peoples that Rome had subjected he mentions the Gauls, who, with so many natural defenses, three hundred and five peoples and their own wealth, and after resisting, he says, eighty years of war, put up with being a source of revenue for Rome, guarded by only twelve hundred soldiers, “scarcely more than their cities.” It is testimony of how a pacified Gaul looked from the East, a century after Caesar.

hechos/estrabon-describe-a-los-habitante.texto: Strabo describes the inhabitants of Ierne

In Book IV of his Geography (IV.5.4), written around the year 18, Strabo says that the inhabitants of Ierne, the island north of Britain, eat human flesh and have intercourse with their mothers and sisters, and at once makes clear that he has no trustworthy witnesses. He adds that it is considered honorable to eat dead fathers, and qualifies the cannibalism: he says it is also told of the Scythians, and that in sieges even Celts and Iberians would have done it. Strabo was never in Ireland and takes this from others: it is the Greco-Roman commonplace about the people at the edge of the world, not an observation.
